enhanced_information: Anatomical dead space refers to the volume of air in the respiratory system that does not participate in gas exchange, primarily consisting of the conducting airways such as the trachea and bronchi. It does not include the alveoli, which are the sites of gas exchange. Anatomical dead space is not always greater than physiological dead space, as physiological dead space includes both anatomical dead space and any alveolar dead space. It does not include medium-sized bronchioles, as they are part of the respiratory zone where gas exchange begins. Additionally, anatomical dead space does not allow for gaseous exchange and is not related to surfactants, which are substances that reduce surface tension in the alveoli. The volume of anatomical dead space is distinct from inspiratory reserve volume, which is the additional air that can be inhaled after a normal inhalation.
